title: Indians Are Paying ₹7 Lakh to Walk the Cannes Red Carpet. Some of Them Are Getting Scammed. Most of Them Don't Care About the Films.
excerpt: A thriving black market in red carpet tickets, complete with hair-and-makeup packages and Getty photographers, has turned 'India at Cannes' into a status symbol for sale. Organisers are vanishing. Attendees are stranded. And the real Indian filmmakers are being drowned out.
body:
Every May, a particular genre of Instagram post floods NRI feeds: an Indian influencer, designer, or businessperson on the Cannes red carpet, tagged with some version of "representing India at the world's biggest film festival."

This year, the Hollywood Reporter India published a devastating investigation into what those posts actually represent. The answer, increasingly, is money.

The Price List

According to reporting by Ananya Shankar, red carpet access at Cannes starts at approximately €5,750 (₹5.5 lakh) for balcony seating at major premieres. Premium orchestra and corbeille access goes up to €7,250 (₹7 lakh). The full package — including hair and makeup at the hotel, a limousine to the carpet, a set of professional photographs, and optional Getty photographer services — can cost over $10,000.

None of this requires any connection to the film industry. You don't need to have made a film, acted in one, or even seen one at the festival. You just need a credit card.

The Scam Layer

But beneath the legitimate (if morally questionable) ticket market lies something worse: outright fraud.

Pankhuri Harikrishnan, founder of Fetch India and a Cannes regular since 2018, told the Hollywood Reporter India that she received calls from multiple people who had flown to Cannes on the promise of red carpet access, only to find their organisers had vanished.

"I've been called by various individuals who had been promised carpet appearances, but after they have landed in Cannes… the organisers vanished," she said. Some were told they could walk the carpet at 11 AM — which is when it sits empty, between screenings. They arrived in rented designer outfits with no tickets, no contacts, and no plan.

The Self-Funded Narrative

Harikrishnan's sharpest observation isn't about the scams. It's about the ecosystem that makes them possible.

"Not only are you getting access because you can buy it, you're also getting media attention because you can buy that too," she says. "Together, therefore, you're creating a narrative that's completely self-funded."

The result: NRI audiences scrolling through their feeds see a flood of "India at Cannes" content that has nothing to do with Indian cinema. The people in those photos aren't there for the films. They don't want tickets to screenings. They want photos on the carpet.

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For NRIs who genuinely care about Indian cinema's global standing, this is embarrassing. While Payal Kapadia was running the Critics' Week jury — a position of real institutional power — and an FTII student's Punjabi film was screening in the official selection, the dominant "India at Cannes" narrative on social media was still about outfits, influencer collaborations, and purchased access.

Harikrishnan put it bluntly on Instagram: "We are just giving India a terrible, terrible name at an international platform."

The problem isn't that influencers exist at Cannes. Fashion brands have legitimate partnerships with the festival. L'Oréal Paris brings ambassadors like Aishwarya Rai Bachchan to the carpet every year — and Aishwarya turned heads again this year at the closing ceremony. That's above board.

The problem is the grey market below it: unaffiliated individuals and agencies selling carpet access to anyone who'll pay, creating a funnel that overwhelms the legitimate Indian presence with noise.

What Can Change?

Probably very little. As Harikrishnan admits, the demand drives the supply. As long as walking the Cannes red carpet is seen as a status symbol in India — and as long as social media makes it possible to monetise that symbol — the market will exist.

But NRI audiences can at least learn to distinguish between the two kinds of "India at Cannes" stories: the ones involving actual filmmakers with actual films, and the ones involving rented dresses and vanishing organisers.

The former is growing. The latter is just louder.
nri_angle: NRIs in the UK, US, and Canada see 'India at Cannes' headlines on their feeds constantly. This story peels back what those headlines actually represent: a pay-to-play ecosystem where proximity to the red carpet has become a commodity, often at the expense of legitimate Indian filmmakers trying to be taken seriously.
author: Diaspora Desk
